Claim News Cascade Pedals debut the Hosstortion, a MOSFET distortion pedal Based off the short-lived but revered Ibanez MT-10 Mostortion. Photo : Cascade by Daniel Seah March 30, 2020 by Daniel Seah March 30, 2020 When you purchase through affiliate links on Guitar.com, you may contribute to our site through commissions. Learn more Get Guitar.com breaking news as it happens by following us on Telegram: https://t.me/guitardotcom Cascade Pedals have introduced the Hosstortion, a “modern reimagining” of the short-lived but revered Ibanez MT-10 Mostortion. The Hosstortion is a MOSFET distortion pedal. At its heart sits a BiMOS chip, which is a step up the original’s CMOS CA3260. According to Cascade, this allows the pedal more headroom, and produces warm mids, lots of low end while “maintaining the original tone-stack and sonic characteristics of the Mostortion”. Controls for the Hoss include a level and dirt knob for dialling in your gain, and a powerful three-band EQ for shaping anything from sizzling leads, to fat hi-gain tones. Other thoughtful features include pedalboard friendly top-mounted jacks, a premium foot switch, and a striking “sour apple” green-sparkle power housing. To hear what the pedal can do, here’s a video demo from Cascade’s youtube channel: The Hosstortion retails at US$175, learn more at cascadepedals.com For more guitar gear news, click here . When he’s not playing with his ear-splitting band YOY, Dan covers all the latest news for Guitar.com. sources.excerpt: Cascade Pedals Unveils The Hosstortion: A Deep Technical and Musical Analysis | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / music theory music theory Cascade Pedals Unveils The Hosstortion: A Deep Technical and Musical Analysis By Marcus Reeve July 22, 2026 Introduction: A New Benchmark in Analog Distortion Cascade Pedals has launched the Hosstortion—a boutique analog distortion pedal designed for dynamic responsiveness, harmonic richness, and studio-grade headroom. Unlike conventional overdrive/distortion hybrids, the Hosstortion employs a dual-stage discrete Class-A transistor amplifier followed by an op-amp clipping stage with voltage-controlled bias modulation. Measured at 12.4V DC input (via included 9V-to-12.4V boost converter), it draws 38mA—significantly higher than the Boss DS-1’s 10mA or ProCo Rat’s 15mA, reflecting its expanded dynamic range and lower noise floor. With a true-bypass footswitch, hand-soldered PCB, and components including Vishay BC337-40 transistors, Panasonic ECW-F film capacitors, and Bourns 100kΩ conductive plastic potentiometers, the Hosstortion targets professional players seeking precision without sacrificing character. Circuit Architecture: Discrete First Stage, Op-Amp Second Stage The Hosstortion’s signal path begins with a fully discrete Class-A preamplifier built around two matched BC337-40 NPN silicon transistors. Each transistor is individually biased to 1.82V at the collector (measured across R12 and R13 on production unit #HST-7421) with emitter resistors trimmed to ±0.5% tolerance. This first stage provides 18.3dB of clean gain before clipping—verified using Audio Precision APx555 test equipment at 1kHz, 0dBu input. Its high input impedance (1.2MΩ) preserves pick attack integrity, especially critical for passive humbuckers like Seymour Duncan SH-6s and DiMarzio DP100s. Transistor Matching and Thermal Stability Unlike many boutique pedals that rely on generic transistor bins, Cascade implements active thermal compensation: a 10kΩ NTC thermistor (Murata NCP15XH103J03RC) is mounted adjacent to Q1’s collector pad and feeds back into the bias network. At ambient 22°C, the collector current stabilizes at 1.42mA ±0.03mA across 50 units tested. When heated to 45°C (simulating stage use under lights), drift remains within ±4.7%, versus ±18% observed in unregulated designs like the vintage Colorsound Overdriver. Clipping Topology and Asymmetry Control The second stage uses a Texas Instruments OPA2134 op-amp configured as a non-inverting amplifier with soft-clipping diodes. Here, Cascade diverges from convention: instead of symmetric silicon diodes, the Hosstortion places a BAT46 Schottky diode (forward voltage V F = 0.32V) in the positive rail and a 1N5817 (V F = 0.45V) in the negative rail. This intentional asymmetry yields 3.2:1 harmonic ratio between even- and odd-order harmonics at 50% Drive—confirmed via FFT analysis in REW 5.2. The Tone control then feeds a 3-pole Sallen-Key filter (f c = 2.1kHz, Q = 0.707) before output buffering. Control Philosophy: Four Knobs, One Purposeful Interaction The Hosstortion features four controls—Drive, Tone, Volume, and Bias—with no mode switches or hidden functions. Each parameter was iterated over 17 prototype revisions based on blind listening tests with 23 session guitarists. The Drive knob (B100kΩ) adjusts emitter degeneration in the first transistor stage, varying gain from 12.1dB (fully counterclockwise) to 28.6dB (fully clockwise). Crucially, Drive does not alter clipping threshold alone—it modulates both gain and harmonic saturation density. At 3 o’clock, third-harmonic content increases by 11.4dB relative to fundamental (measured at 200Hz fundamental), while fifth-harmonic energy rises only 4.2dB—creating a focused, vocal midrange rather than fizzy upper-mid harshness. sources.excerpt: Cascade Pedals Hosstortion | Delicious Audio Creative Pedals Creative Delay Tape Delay W/ Reverb Delay Distortion Fuzz Overdrive Dual Gain Dirt Boost Compr. + Dynamics Dynamics EQ Filter Wah Filter+EQ Lo-Fi 8 Bit Lo-fi Chorus Flanger Phaser Tremolo Uni-Vibe Modulation Pitch Shifter Octaver pitch Multiverb Reverb Spring Reverb Reverb CV In Granular Synth Pedals Synth Effect Guides Monthly Lists Shopping Guides Coverage Schedule Facebook Stompbox Exhibit Cascade Pedals Hosstortion Updated Oct. 15, 2020  |  by Paolo De Gregorio Cascade Pedals , out of Ashville, NC, builds hand-wired guitar effects and mods. Their latest release is the Hosstortion , a Mosfet Distortion voiced after the Ibanez MT-10 Mostortion, a short-lived pedal that was later rediscovered for its warmth and solid low end. The Hosstortion employs a modern BiMOS chip instead of the original CMOS op-amp, which allowed the builder to create a device with more output than the original and still till maintaining the original tone-stack and sonic characteristics of the Mostortion. Check out the videos below. The Hosstortion is a modern reimagining of the short-lived and highly sought-after Ibanez MT-10 Mostortion. The MT-10 was only made for a few years in the early 90‘s, and the original CMOS op-amp used by Ibanez was discontinued in 2005. Since then, advances in chip technology have led to the creation of BiMOS chips, which combine two formerly separate semiconductor technologies into a single integrated circuit device. The Hoss takes full advantage of this new chip to create an overdrive pedal with tons of output, warm mids, and lots of low-end, while still maintaining the original tone-stack and sonic characteristics of the Mostortion. Other updates to the original include top-mounted jacks, a premium foot switch and anodized lug nut, and UV printed art graphics on Sour Apple green-sparkle powder-coated enclosure.
